rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crops ‘eat’ metaphorically because they are consumed during those years, as in describing day as seeing.
rows.anchor: الأكل الذي في قوله: يأكلن على سبيل المجاز من حيث أنه يؤكل فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥṣinūn means preserve and store, deriving from ḥiṣn, a refuge or fortress.
rows.anchor: ومعنى تحصنون تحرزون وتخبئون، مأخوذ من الحصن وهو الحرز والملجأ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والجمهور
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and most exegetes derive yughāth from rain; another view derives it from relief.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد والجمهور: يغاث من الغيث، وقيل: من الغوث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain derivation is triliteral, while the relief derivation is quadriliteral.
rows.anchor: ففي الأول بني من ثلاثي، وفي الثاني من رباعي

rows.speaker: الأخوان
rows.claim: The two readers use second-person taʿṣirūn; the other seven use third-person yaʿṣirūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان: تعصرون بالتاء على الخطاب، وباقي السبعة بالياء على الغيبة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read the verb as squeezing plants and produce, including grapes, cane, olives, sesame, radish, and milk.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أنه من عصر النبات كالعنب والقصب والزيتون والسمسم والفجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says people pressed nothing during the drought years.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم لم يعصروا شيئا مدة الجدب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وغيره
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and others derive the word from ʿaṣra, deliverance, and cite Abu Zubayd’s verse about Uthman as refuge for the distressed.
rows.anchor: والعصر وهو المنجي، ومنه قول أبي زبيد

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد، والأعرج، وعيسى البصرة
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿraj, and ʿIsa of Basra read a passive form, meaning people are delivered from hardship, matching yughāth.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر بن محمد، والأعرج، وعيسى البصرة يعصرون بضم الياء وفتح الصاد مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: A second reading from ʿIsa uses second-person passive taʿṣarūn, likewise meaning you are rescued from hardship.
rows.anchor: وعن عيسى أيضا: تعصرون بالتاء على الخطاب مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: ابن المستنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mustanir reads it as rain falling on people, from a cloud releasing its water, with the action figuratively attributed to them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المستنير: معناه يمطرون، من أعصرت السحابة ماءها عليهم

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash reports a doubled, intensive reading of yaʿṣirūn.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش أنه قرىء يعصرون بضم الياء وكسر الصاد وشدها، من عصر مشددا للتكثير

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads taʿtaṣirūn, formed by assimilating tāʾ into ṣād; it may mean squeezing or being delivered.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: وفيه تعصرون، بكسر التاء والعين والصاد وشدها، وأصله تعتصرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph interpreted the fat cows and green ears as fertile years, and the lean cows and dry ears as drought years.
rows.anchor: تأول يوسف عليه السلام البقرات السمان والسنبلات الخضر بسين مخصبة، والعجاف واليابسات بسنين مجدبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After interpreting the dream, Joseph announced a blessed, abundant eighth year through revelation.
rows.anchor: ثم بشرهم بعد الفراغ من تأويل الرؤيا بمجيء العام الثامن مباركا خصيبا كثير الخير

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God gave Joseph knowledge of an additional year; revelation specified the eighth year’s abundance, already expected after seven severe years.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة: زاده الله علم سنة، والذي من جهة الوحي هو التفضيل بحال العام

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya supplies omitted events: the messenger reported Joseph’s interpretation, and the king and court admired his insight and truthfulness.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: في تضاعيف هذه الآيات محذوفات يعطيها ظاهر الكلام ويدل عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Impressed by Joseph’s interpretation and reputation for truth, the king ordered that he be brought to him.
rows.anchor: فعظم يوسف في نفس الملك وقال: ائتوني به

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Joseph asked the king to investigate the women so he could determine whether the imprisonment was just.
rows.anchor: ومقصد يوسف عليه السلام إنما كان وقل له يستقصي عن ذنبي، وينظر في أمري، هل سجنت بحق أو بظلم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya describes Joseph’s delay as patience and a demand to clear his name before accepting royal rank.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا الفعل من يوسف إناءة وصبرا وطلبا لبراءة الساحة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Joseph feared leaving prison and gaining favor while his religion and reputation remained unvindicated, so people would always regard him as the man who pursued his master’s wife.
rows.anchor: خشي أن يخرج وينال من الملك مرتبة، ويسكت عن أمر دينه صفحا، فيراه الناس بتلك العين أبدا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Joseph waited to establish his innocence and forestall envious people using the imprisonment to lower his standing.
rows.anchor: إنما تأنى وتثبت في إجابة الملك، وقدم سؤال النسوة لتظهر براءة ساحته

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari draws a principle that one should dispel suspicion and avoid places where accusations arise.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على أن الاجتهاد في نفي التهم واجبة وجوب إبقاء الوقوف في مواقفها

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted warning believers not to stand in places that invite suspicion.
rows.anchor: من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فلا يقفن مواقف التهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reportedly showed judges a written statement that his amputated leg was not cut for treachery or corruption, warding off suspicion.
rows.anchor: وكان مقطوع الرجل قد أثبت على القضاة أن رجله لم تقطع في خيانة ولا فساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asked about the women rather than directly ordering a search because a question would prompt the king to investigate and expose the truth.
rows.anchor: لأن السؤال مما يهيج الإنسان ويحركه للبحث عنما سئل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s question sought a full account that would make his innocence unmistakable and distinguish truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: ليجري التفتيش عن حقيقة القصة، وقص الحديث حتى يتبين له براءته بيانا مكشوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s restraint and generosity appear in his not naming the wife of al-Aziz despite her role in his imprisonment.
rows.anchor: ومن كرم يوسف عليه السلام أنه لم يذكر زوج العزيز مع ما صنعت به

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abu Haywa and Abu Bakr from Asim read al-niswah with a ḍamma on the nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة وأبو بكر عن عاصم في رواية النسوة بضم النون

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group read al-lāʾi, and both forms are plurals of allatī.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة اللاي بالياء، وكلاهما جمع التي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s statement that God knows their plotting may testify to the scheme’s gravity and his innocence, threaten them, or imply divine recompense.
rows.anchor: أراد أن كيدهن عظيم لا يعلمه إلا الله لبعد عوده، واستشهد بعلم الله على أنهن كدنه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows rabb to mean Joseph’s master, al-Aziz, as an appeal and reproach.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن يريد بالرب العزيز مولاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Aziz as the referent of rabb; ‘their plotting’ refers specifically to the women under inquiry.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره ابن عطية من هذا الاحتمال لا يسوغ، والضمير في بكيدهن عائد على النسوة المذكورات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king’s question follows an omitted return and report by the messenger; he gathered the women and al-Aziz’s wife to recount the case.
rows.anchor: ما خطبكن في الكلام حذف تقديره: فرجع الرسول فأخبره بما قال يوسف، فجمع الملك النسوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king frames the matter as their solicitation of Joseph; their urging him to obey their mistress was their attempt.
rows.anchor: ونزه جانب يوسف بقوله: إذ راودتن يوسف عن نفسه، ومراودتهن له قولهن ليوسف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads their exclamation as amazement at Joseph’s chastity and distance from suspicion.
rows.anchor: لكن قلن: حاش لله تعجبا من عفته، وذهابه بنفسه عن شيء من الريبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s integrity can be attributed to God’s guidance and protection; he then humbles himself instead of claiming complete innocence.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون توكيدا لأمانته، وأنه لو كان خائنا لما هدى الله كيده، ولا سدده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘I do not absolve myself’ denies total self-vindication, since the human soul urges toward evil and desire.
rows.anchor: فقال: وما أبرىء نفسي من الزلل، وما أشهد لها بالبراءة الكلية، ولا أزكيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author criticizes al-Zamakhshari’s expansion of the generic statement about the soul as imposing more on the wording than it carries.
rows.anchor: أراد الجنس أي: هذا الجنس يأمر بالسوء، ويحمل على ما فيه من الشهوات انتهى. وفيه تكثير وتحميل للفظ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues the statement can be Joseph’s despite lacking an explicit speech tag, since its meaning guides that attribution.
rows.anchor: كفى بالمعنى دليلا قائدا إلى أن يجعل من كلامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Zamakhshari’s parallel from Pharaoh’s speech: the disputed clause could instead be the courtiers speaking among themselves.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس كما ذكر، إذ لا يتعين في هذا التركيب أن يكون من كلام فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bi-l-ghayb may be circumstantial of the subject or object, or an adverb meaning in the unseen.
rows.anchor: وبالغيب يحتمل أن يكون حالا من الفاعل أي: غائبا عنه، أو من المفعول أي: غائبا عني

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: The exception may be connected to the soul or its omitted object, to an implied time span, or disconnected; Ibn Atiyya says the last is the majority view.
rows.anchor: وجوزوا أن يكون استثناء منقطعا، وما مصدرية. وذكر ابن عطية أنه قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits the king hearing the women’s testimony and summoning Joseph; the speaker when they conversed may be the king or Joseph.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الفاعل بكلمة هو ضمير الملك أي: فلما كلمه الملك ورأى حسن جوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Joseph may be the subject of ‘when he spoke with him,’ and the king admired his speech.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون الفاعل ضمير يوسف أي: فلما كلم يوسف الملك، ورأى الملك حسن منطقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king calls Joseph established and trusted; trustworthiness is more honoring than reading amīn as merely safe.
rows.anchor: أي: ذو مكانة ومنزلة، أمين مؤتمن على كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asks to administer the stores because he is dependable and knowledgeable in management, the qualities rulers need.
rows.anchor: وصف نفسه بالأمانة والكفاءة وهما مقصود الملوك ممن يولونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects restricting ḥafīẓ to accounting and ʿalīm to languages or famine expertise.
rows.anchor: وهذا التخصيص لا وجه له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may praise himself truthfully when others do not know his qualifications; this is not forbidden self-purification.
rows.anchor: أنه يجوز للإنسان أن يثني على نفسه بالحق إذا جهل أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A righteous person may serve a merchant or ruler in accord with religious law and justice, not unlawful preferences.
rows.anchor: وعلى جواز عمل الرجل الصالح للرجل التاجر بما يقتضيه الشرع والعدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sought office to enact God’s judgment, establish justice, and perform a task no one else could do as well.
rows.anchor: وإنما طلب يوسف هذه الولاية ليتوصل إلى إمضاء حكم الله، وإقامة الحق، وبسط العدل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reports that the king had become Muslim; if so, Joseph’s appointment poses no issue.
rows.anchor: فإن كان الملك قد أسلم كما روى مجاهد فلا كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the king was unbelieving, an official may seek his support when needed to enforce God’s law and remove injustice.
rows.anchor: وإن كان كافرا ولا سبيل إلى الحكم بأمر الله ودفع الظلم إلا بتمكينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the king deferred to Joseph’s judgment and followed his decisions.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان الملك يصدر عن رأي يوسف ولا يعترض عليه في كل ما رأى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes Joseph’s elevation, marriage, justice, conversions, grain sales through successive forms of payment, and eventual release of Egypt’s people and restoration of their property.
rows.anchor: روي أن الملك توجه بتاجه، وختمه بخاتمه، ورداه بسيفه، ووضع له سريرا من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says Joseph capped purchases at one camel-load per person and that famine reached Canaan and Syria, prompting Jacob to send his sons while retaining Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وكان لا يبيع من أحد من الممتارين أكثر من حمل بعير تقسيطا بين الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report concludes that Joseph freed Egypt’s people and returned their property after the king accepted his judgment.
rows.anchor: فإني أشهد الله وأشهدك أني أعتقت أهل مصر عن آخرهم، ورددت عليهم أملاكهم

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن كثير وأبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع
rows.claim: Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, and Nafiʿ read nashāʾ with first-person plural nūn; most use third-person yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن كثير: بخلاف عنهم أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع: حيث نشاء بالنون، والجمهور بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With yāʾ, the subject may be Joseph, whose will follows God’s, or God, expressed by a shift in address.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قراءة الياء يكون فاعل نشاء ضميرا يعود على يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s mercy includes blessing through kingship and wealth; reward for good is not lost in this world, while the afterlife reward lasts.
rows.anchor: نصيب برحمتنا أي: بنعمتنا من الملك والغنى وغيرهما، ولا نضيع في الدنيا أجر من أحسن

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna says believers receive good deeds’ reward in both lives, while the wicked get worldly good early and no share hereafter; a hadith supports him.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة: المؤمن يثاب على حسناته في الدنيا والآخرة، والفاجر يعجل له الخير في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse signals that Joseph’s afterlife state is better than his impressive worldly position.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية إشارة إلى أن حال يوسف في الآخرة خير من حالته العظيمة في الدنيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari’s account says Joseph required their youngest brother as proof and held Simeon hostage by lot; another report says he held no one.
rows.anchor: فاقترعوا فأصاب القرعة شمعون، وكان أحسنهم رأيا في يوسف، فخلفوه عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another story says Joseph tested truth by tapping the cup, then suspected the brothers when they said a wolf ate their brother.
rows.anchor: وكان ينقر في الصواع فيفهم من طنينه صدق الحديث أو كذبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has kasra on the jīm of jihāz.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: بجهازهم بكسر الجيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says ‘a brother’ rather than ‘your brother’ to conceal his recognition of them; definiteness signals a shared known referent, while indefinite wording can still describe someone the speaker knows.
rows.anchor: وتنكر أخ، ولم يقل بأخيكم وإن كان قد عرفه وعرفهم مبالغة في كونه لا يريد أن يتعرف لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s full measure and hospitality reassure and persuade them to bring their brother; he threatens to deny them future grain if they fail.
rows.anchor: ألا ترون أني أوف الكيل وأنا خير المنزلين أي المضيفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-lā taqrabūn may be a prohibition or an independent negative with prohibitive force, with alternative grammatical analyses.
rows.anchor: واحتمل قوله: ولا تقربون، أن يكون نهيا، وأن يكون نفيا مستقلا ومعناه النهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s dealings appear to follow revelation; otherwise kindness would call for summoning Jacob, but God intended Jacob’s trial and the first dream’s fulfilment.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كل ما فعله يوسف عليه السلام معهم أنه بوحي، وإلا فإنه كان مقتضى البر أن يبادر إلى أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers that the withheld measure was Benjamin’s camel-load, which he missed because he was absent, rather than a future refusal of grain.
rows.anchor: وهذا أولى بحمل منع على الماضي حقيقة، ولقولهم: فأرسل معنا أخانا نكتل

rows.speaker: الأخوان
rows.claim: The two readers use yaktal, meaning their brother would obtain the measure; the other seven use naktal for the brothers’ need.
rows.anchor: ويقويه قراءة يكتل بالياء أي: يكتل أخونا

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The other seven read naktal with nūn, meaning the brothers will obtain the food they need.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة بالنون أي: نرفع المانع من الكيل، أو نكتل من الطعام ما نحتاج إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s ‘will I trust you?’ reminds them he had entrusted Joseph to them with the same promise of protection.
rows.anchor: هذا توقيف وتقرير. وتألم من فراقه بنيامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob fears they may harm Benjamin as before, but does not forbid the journey because he sees a benefit; he entrusts Benjamin to God.
rows.anchor: قلتم فيه: وإنا له لحافظون، كما قلتم في هذا، فأخاف أن تكيدوا له

rows.speaker: الأخوان وحفص
rows.claim: The two readers and Hafs read ḥāfiẓan as an active participle; the author parses it and ḥifẓan as specification of the kind of protection.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان وحفص: حافظا اسم فاعل، وانتصب حفظا وحافظا على التمييز

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows ḥāfiẓan as a circumstantial accusative, but the author rejects it as limiting God’s good protection.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الزمخشري أن يكون حافظا حالا، وليس بجيد، لأن فيه تقييد خير بهذه الحال

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads ‘better protector’ in an annexation construction, emphasizing that God surpasses every protector.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: خير حافظ على الإضافة، فالله تعالى متصف بالحفظ وزيادته على كل حافظ

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra is reported to read khayr al-ḥāfiẓīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو هريرة: خير الحافظين، كذا نقل الزمخشري

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reports Ibn Masʿud’s expanded wording, which should be explanatory rather than Qurʾanic text.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وقرأ ابن مسعود، فالله خير حافظا وهو خير الحافظين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s appeal to God as most merciful expresses hope for Benjamin’s protection and that he will not suffer a second loss.
rows.anchor: وهو أرحم الراحمين اعتراف بأن الله هو ذو الرحمة الواسعة، فأرجو منه حفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muzjāh is inferior merchandise traders push away in scorn; the root also describes wind driving clouds, illustrated by Hatim al-Taʾi’s poem about a rejected guest.
rows.anchor: المزجاة: المدفوعة يدفعها كل تاجر رغبة عنها واحتقارا من أزجيته إذا دفعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Īthār broadly means favor and all kinds of gifts.
rows.anchor: الإيثار: لفظ يعم جميع التفضل وأنواع العطايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tathrīb is reproach or blame; some gloss it as taunting.
rows.anchor: التثريب: التأنيب والعتب، وعبر بعضهم عنه بالتعيير

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith is quoted instructing that a slave girl who commits fornication be whipped without reproach.
rows.anchor: إذا زنت أمة أحدكم فليجلدها ولا يثرب

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Joseph burst into tears when the brothers pleaded hardship, then began revealing himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق: وارفض دمعه باكيا، فشرع في كشف أمره إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s question concerns their separating him in childhood and mistreating Benjamin after Joseph disappeared.
rows.anchor: أي: من التفريق بينهما في الصغر، وإذاية بنيامين بعد مغيب يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya explains ‘ignorant’ as either ignorance of sin or lack of judgment and prudence.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ونسبهم إما إلى جهل المعصية، وإما إلى جهل السيئات وقلة الحنكة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads Joseph’s question as religious counsel: did they recognize the wrong and repent, since knowing its ugliness leads to repentance?
rows.anchor: فكان كلامه شفقة عليهم وتنصحا لهم في الدين، وإيثارا لحق الله على حق نفسه

rows.speaker: قول الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority understands ‘did you know?’ as a rebuking question that magnifies the enormity of what they did.
rows.anchor: قول الجمهور: هل علمتم استفهام معناه التقريع والتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph avoids repeating their accusation against Benjamin in front of them, honoring Jacob by not including him in the same account.
rows.anchor: تعظيما لقدره وتفخيما لشأنه أن يذكره مع نفسه وأخيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan say ‘ignorant’ means they were children.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، والحسن: جاهلون صبيان

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil begins a gloss at the end of this segment; its continuation calls them sinners.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، والحسن: جاهلون صبيان. وقال مقاتل:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations are ignorance of filial duty and kinship, surrender to desire, not foreseeing Joseph’s fate, or failing to consider consequences and interests.
rows.anchor: جاهلون بما يجب من بر الأب، وصلة الرحم، وترك الهوى

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes say Joseph intended to rebuke his brothers for what they did to their father and brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال المفسرون: وغرض يوسف توبيخ إخوته وتأنيبهم على ما فعلوا في حق أبيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers that Joseph was comforting them and easing their guilt by attributing their deed to childish ignorance or delusion.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه قال ذلك تأنيسا لقلوبهم، وبسط عذر كأنه قال: إنما أقدمكم على ذلك الفعل القبيح جهالة الصبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects stories that Joseph crucified his brothers or ordered their execution as unsound and contrary to his compassionate character.
rows.anchor: لا يصح البتة، وكان يوسف من أرق خلق الله وأشفقهم على الأجانب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers recognized that the speaker knew their history; one report says he lifted the screen and crown, revealing the family mark and his identity.
rows.anchor: فرفعه ووضع التاج وتبسم، وكان يضيء ما حوله من نور تبسمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view calls their question confirmation because they already knew him by signs mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استفهام تقرير، لأنهم كانوا عرفوه بتلك العلامات التي سبق ذكرها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says his appearance and manner of speech revealed him as a Muslim descendant of Abraham rather than an Egyptian notable.
rows.anchor: رأوا في روائه وشمائله حين كلمهم بذلك ما شعروا به أنه هو

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce the question with an interrogative hamza; readings differ in how the two hamzas are realized or softened.
rows.anchor: الاستفهام، والخلاف في تحقيق الهمزتين، أو تليين الثانية

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن محيصن وابن كثير
rows.claim: Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Kathir read innaka without the interrogative hamza, which is apparently understood rather than a plain assertion.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة، وابن محيصن، وابن كثير: إنك بغير همزة استفهام، والظاهر أنها مرادة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy has a reading adding ‘or are you Joseph?’; grammarians supply a deleted predicate or repeat the name, which al-Zamakhshari takes as startled insistence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: أإنك، أو أنت يوسف

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s reading asks, ‘or are you Joseph?’
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي بن كعب قالوا: أو أنت يوسف؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the common reading, the emphatic lām may mark separation before the predicate or appear with anta as subject; anta cannot be emphatic because the lām intervenes.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة الجمهور: أإنك لأنت، يجوز أن تكون اللام دخلت على أنت، وهو فصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph identifies Benjamin because the earlier question mentioned them together, then credits God with their reunion and comfort after estrangement.
rows.anchor: وزادهم في الجواب قوله: وهذا أخي، لأنه سبق قوله: هل علمتم ما فعلتم بيوسف وأخيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers taking piety and patience generally, rather than restricting them to Joseph’s ordeals.
rows.anchor: والأحسن أن لا تخص التقوى بحالة ولا الصبر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets piety as leaving sin and patience as enduring prison.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: من يتقي في تركه المعصية ويصبر في السجن

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿi interprets the pair as avoiding adultery and bearing celibacy.
rows.anchor: وقال النخعي: من يتقي الزنا ويصبر على العزوبة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes it as fearing God and punishment, refraining from sins, and persevering in obedience.
rows.anchor: من يتق، من يخف الله وعقابه، ويصبر عن المعاصي، وعلى الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses tie piety and patience to calamities or people’s harm; the author says these are specifications drawn from Joseph’s circumstances.
rows.anchor: وهذه كلها تخصيصات بحسب حالة يوسف ونوازله

rows.speaker: قنبل
rows.claim: For Qunbul’s yatqī, the author prefers a jussive with deleted final yāʾ on a rare but reported dialect, rejecting Abu Ali’s restriction to poetry.
rows.anchor: والأحسن من هذه الأقوال أن يكون يتقي مجزوما على لغة، وإن كانت قليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muḥsinīn may be general or replace a pronoun because it encompasses the pious and patient; the meaning is that their reward is not lost.
rows.anchor: والمحسنين: عام يندرج فيه من تقدم، أو وضع موضع الضمير لاشتماله على المتقين والصابرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God favored Joseph with kingship, patience, and knowledge.
rows.anchor: فضلك بالملك، أو بالصبر، والعلم قالهما ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
rows.claim: Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi says God favored Joseph with forbearance and forgiveness.
rows.anchor: أو بالحلم والصفح ذكره أبو سليمان الدمشقي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari relates God’s favor to piety, patience, and the conduct of the good, matching the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: قاله: الزمخشري، وهو مناسب لقوله: إنه من يتق الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ confession that Joseph was favored also seeks to elicit his kindness and acknowledges their wrong.
rows.anchor: وخطابهم إياه بذلك استنزال لإحسانه، واعتراف بما صدر منهم في حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāṭiʾīn describes deliberate wrongdoing, whereas akhṭaʾ describes aiming at what is right but failing to attain it.
rows.anchor: وخاطئين: من خطىء إذا تعمد. وأما أخطأ فقصد الصواب ولم يوفق له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā tathrīb means no blame or punishment; yawm may attach to a phrase of stability or to God’s forgiveness.
rows.anchor: ولا تثريب: لا لوم ولا عقوبة. وتثريب اسم لا، وعليكم الخبر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari offers three possible attachments for ‘today,’ explaining it as the day when blame would ordinarily be expected.
rows.anchor: بالتثريب، أو بالمقدر في عليكم من معنى الاستقرار، أو بيغفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects attaching ‘today’ directly to tathrīb: a verbal noun and its complement cannot be separated, and this parse would make yawm declinable.
rows.anchor: هذا لا يجوز، لأن التثريب مصدر، وقد فصل بينه وبين معموله بقوله: وعليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers attaching ‘today’ to an omitted stability predicate and starting yaghfir as a prayer; Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari support this reading.
rows.anchor: ولذلك وقف على قوله اليوم أكثر القراء. وابتدأوا بيغفر الله لكم على جهة الدعاء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers pausing at ‘today,’ since otherwise Joseph would assert God’s forgiveness unless it came by revelation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والوقف على اليوم أرجح في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes that reading forgiveness as certain follows a Muʿtazili premise that forgiveness requires repentance; Ibn al-Anbari says this is the first moment of pardon.
rows.anchor: فبشارة إلى آخره، فعلى طريق المعتزلة، فإن الغفران لا يكون إلا لمن تاب

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hawfi parses ʿalaykum as an adjective modifying tathrīb, with al-yawm as predicate; the author calls it a good analysis.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الحوفي أن يكون عليكم في موضع الصفة لتثريب، ويكون الخبر اليوم، وهو وجه حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A strong alternative supplies ‘no reproach will reproach you today,’ making the omitted predicate govern the day; Arabic often omits a known predicate after lā.
rows.anchor: لكان وجها قويا، لأن خبر لا إذا علم كثر حذفه عند أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph invokes God as most merciful because mercy is the reason he hopes God will accept his prayer for forgiveness.
rows.anchor: أخبر عن الله بالصفة التي هي سبب الغفران، وهو أنه تعالى أرحم الرحماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in ‘with my shirt’ most naturally marks accompanying circumstance, though it may mean ‘carry my shirt.’
rows.anchor: والباء في بقميصي الظاهر أنها للحال أي: مصحوبين أو ملتبسين به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One story says Joseph’s shirt was inherited and came from paradise through Gabriel, healing afflicted people by its scent.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو القميص الذي توارثه يوسف وكان في عنقه، وكان من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account traces the garment from Abraham, whom God clothed with it after the fire, through Isaac and Jacob to Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان لإبراهيم كساه الله إياه من الجنة حين خرج من النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies it as the shirt torn from behind, showing that Joseph was protected from sexual wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو القميص الذي قد من دبر، أرسله ليعلم يعقوب أنه عصم من الفاحشة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya and the author favor an ordinary shirt Joseph wore; a paradise garment would make Jacob’s distant recognition less surprising, not more.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه قميص من ملبوس يوسف بمنزلة قميص كل واحد، قال ذلك: ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s instruction assumes he knew Jacob had lost his sight from grief, by report or revelation.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه علم أنه عمي من الحزن، إما بإعلامهم، وإما بوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that Jacob would regain sight appears to reflect revelation to Joseph.
rows.anchor: يأت بصيرا، يظهر أنه بوحي

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the family Joseph summoned numbered seventy; other reports say eighty, ninety-three, or ninety-six, with ninety-three attributed to Masruq.
rows.anchor: وأهلوه الذين أمر بأن يؤتى بهم سبعون، أو ثمانون، أو ثلاثة وتسعون، أو ستة وتسعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed family total grew in Egypt until six hundred thousand descendants left with Moses.
rows.anchor: وفي واحد من هذا العدد حلوا بمصر ونموا حتى خرج من ذريتهم مع موسى عليه السلام ستمائة ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʾt means ‘come to me,’ and baṣīran is a circumstantial state.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: يأت، يأتيني، وانتصب بصيرا على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faṣala can mean depart intransitively or separate something transitively; here the caravan set out from Egypt toward Jacob.
rows.anchor: ومعنى فصلت العير: انفصلت من عريش مصر قاصدة مكان يعقوب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas’s reading says the caravan separated; he says Jacob detected Joseph’s scent from eight days away as wind carried it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: ولما انفصل العير، قال ابن عباس: وجد ريحه من مسيرة ثمانية أيام

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن جريج
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj estimate the scent traveled eighty farsakhs; other reports from al-Hasan say thirty days or ten nights, with separation lasting seventy-seven years.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وابن جريج: من ثمانين فرسخا، وكان مدة فراقه منه سبعا وسبعين سنة

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب المهروي
rows.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Mahwuri says the wind asked permission to carry Joseph’s scent to Jacob, and permission was granted.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي أيوب المهروي: أن الريح استأذنت في إيصال عرف يوسف إلى يعقوب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the wind flapped the shirt, spreading the scent of paradise until Jacob recognized it.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: صفقت الريح القميص فراحت روائح الجنة في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lājad means perceiving by smell; a poem illustrates detecting a breeze from the beloved’s land.
rows.anchor: ومعنى لأجد: لأشم فهو وجود حاسة الشم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada gloss tufannidūn as calling Jacob foolish.
rows.anchor: ومعنى تفندون قال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وقتادة: تسفهون

rows.speaker: عطاء وابن جبير
rows.claim: ʿAta and Ibn Jubayr interpret the word as accusing Jacob of lying.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء وابن جبير: تكذبون

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan offers ‘you consider me aged’ as another meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: تهرمون

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والضحاك ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid gloss it as saying Jacob had lost his mind or become senile; other views say disparage, incapacitate, mislead, or accuse him of error.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد، والضحاك ومجاهد أيضا: تقولون ذهب عقلك وخرفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These glosses converge on judging the speaker’s view unsound, from ignorance, bias, falsehood, weakness, or old age.
rows.anchor: وهذه كلها متقاربة في المعنى، وهي راجعة لاعتقاد فساد رأي المفند

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد البلوطي
rows.claim: Munthir ibn Saʿid says shaykh mufannad describes a corrupted judgment, but an old woman is not called mufannadah because she never had an established opinion to lose.
rows.anchor: وقال منذر بن سعيد البلوطي: يقال شج مفند أي: قد فسد رأيه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives tafnīd from old age, fear, and loss of reason, likewise avoiding its use for a woman.
rows.anchor: وقال معناه الزمخشري قال: التفنيد النسبة إلى الفند وهو الخوف وإنكار العقل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies the omitted result of lawlā as ‘you would have believed me if you did not undermine me.’
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: المعنى لولا تفنيدكم إياي لصدقتموني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead proposes that without their accusation Jacob would have told them that the scent showed Joseph was alive.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال: تقديره لولا أن تفندوني لأخبرتكم بكونه حيا لم يمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The addressees are most likely children left at home, though they could be grandchildren and other relatives.
rows.anchor: والمخاطب بقوله: تفندون، الظاهر من تناسق الضمائر أنه عائد على من كان بقي عنده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes their ‘old error’ as Jacob’s mistake, not deviation from guidance.
rows.anchor: والضلال هنا لا يراد به ضد الهدى والرشاد، قال ابن عباس: المعنى إنك لفي خطئك

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil glosses ḍalāl as misery and hardship.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: الشقاء والعناء

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr interprets it as madness, meaning overwhelmed by love.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير: الجنون، ويعني والله أعلم غلبة المحبة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the brothers’ words were harsh and unjust to their father.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: ذلك من الجفاء الذي لا يسوغ لهم مواجهته به

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada calls it a harsh word they should not have addressed to their father, a prophet of God.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال قتادة: قالوا لوالدهم كلمة غليظة لم يكن ينبغي لهم أن يقولوها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says they meant Jacob’s excessive love, constant mention, and hope for Joseph, whom they believed dead.
rows.anchor: لهجك بذكره، ورجائك لقاءه، وكان عندهم أنه قد مات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the bearer was Judah because he had brought the bloodied shirt earlier.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس أن البشير كان يهوذا، لأنه كان جاء بقميص الدم

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الجوهري
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari says Judah volunteered to carry the shirt of joy after once carrying the shirt of affliction; al-Suddi gives the same account.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الفضل الجوهري: قال يهوذا لإخوته: قد علمتم أني ذهبت إليه بقميص القرحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An after lammā is augmentative; the pronoun in ‘he threw it’ most naturally refers to the bearer, though some say Jacob.
rows.anchor: وأن تطرد زيادتها بعد لما، والضمير المستكن في ألقاه عائد على البشير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Face’ may mean the whole face, the eyes, or a part named for the whole.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أريد الوجه كله كما جرت العادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Irtadda is not one of kāna’s sisters here; baṣīran is a circumstantial adjective meaning Jacob returned to his former sight.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنها ليست من أخواتها، فانتصب بصيرا على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects treating baṣīran as an intensive form: here it is the ordinary active participle from baṣura.
rows.anchor: وليس كذلك لأن فعيلا هنا ليس للمبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Jacob asked how Joseph was; learning that Joseph was a Muslim king, he said the blessing was complete.
rows.anchor: قال: على أي دين تركته؟ قال: على الإسلام، قال: الآن تمت النعمة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the bearer had no news to tell Jacob for seven nights, then consoled him about death’s pangs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: لم يجد البشير عند يعقوب شيئا يبيته به

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says Jacob’s sight, strength, youth, and joy returned after blindness, weakness, age, and distress.
rows.anchor: رجع إليه بصره بعد العمى، والقوة بعد الضعف، والشباب بعد الهرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads ‘I know from God what you do not know’ as part of Jacob’s quoted speech, against al-Zamakhshari’s view that it starts a new statement.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: أني أعلم، محكي بالقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What you do not know’ may mean Joseph’s survival and reunion, the dream’s truth, prophetic trials and relief, or knowledge that the angel of death had not taken Jacob’s soul.
rows.anchor: فقيل: ما لا تعلمون من حياة يوسف، وأن الله يجمع بيننا وبينه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Jacob meant his expectation of the dream’s fulfillment, or perhaps simply his good opinion of God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: ما لا تعلمون هو انتظاره لتأويل الرؤيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Jacob’s ‘I told you’ recalls either his claim to smell Joseph or his warning not to despair of God’s relief.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ألم أقل لكم يعني قوله: إني لأجد ريح يوسف، أو قوله: ولا تيأسوا من روح الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Jacob’s sight returned, the brothers asked him to seek forgiveness and admitted their guilt.
rows.anchor: طلبوا منه أن يستغفر لهم الله لذنوبهم، واعترفوا بالخطأ السابق منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawfa gives more gradual easing than the shorter sa; Ibn Masʿud reports Jacob delayed the prayer until dawn.
rows.anchor: وسوف أستغفر لكم: عدة لهم بالاستغفار بسوف، وهي أبلغ في التنفيس من السين

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud says Jacob postponed seeking forgiveness until the predawn hour.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن مسعود: إنه أخر الاستغفار لهم إلى السحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies Joseph’s parents as his father and maternal grandmother; Abdullah’s codex explicitly adds his brothers to those he welcomed.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أبوه وجدته أم أمه، حكاه الزهراوي. وفي مصحف عبد الله آوى إليه أبويه وإخوته

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Joseph told them to enter Egypt while meeting them on the way; their later entrance upon him would then be at temporary lodging.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: قال لهم ذلك وهم في الطريق حين تلقاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation of ‘enter Egypt’ means settle and establish yourselves there.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ادخلوا مصر أي: تمكنوا منها واستقروا فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax connects entry with God’s will, since all events occur by divine will.
rows.anchor: والظاهر تعلق الدخول على مشيئة الله لما أمرهم بالدخول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reconstructs ‘enter Egypt safe, if God wills’ with an omitted result and an inserted conditional clause.
rows.anchor: التقدير ادخلوا مصر إن شاء الله آمنين، إن شاء الله دخلتم آمنين

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Jurayj relocates ‘if God wills’ to Jacob’s later promise; the author calls this interpretation extremely remote and impossible.
rows.anchor: وهذا البدع من التفسير مروي عن ابن جريج، وهو في غاية البعد، بل في غاية الامتناع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿarsh is the king’s throne; Joseph raised his parents to it in his court, though this may have happened before entering Egypt.
rows.anchor: والعرش سرير الملك. ولما دخل يوسف مصر وجلس في مجلسه على سريره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘they fell down’ may include parents and brothers, or only brothers and courtiers while the parents were honored on the throne.
rows.anchor: والضمير في وخروا عائد على أبويه وعلى إخوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning is familiar prostration to Joseph, matching the dream; such prostration was then permitted as a gesture of honor.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: وخروا له سجدا أنه السجود المعهود، وأن الضمير في له عائد على يوسف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says prostration was a customary royal greeting, while God gave this community the greeting of Paradise, peace.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: كانت تحية الملوك عندهم، وأعطى الله هذه الأمة السلام تحية أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects readings of prostration as merely a nod or deep bow because kharrū implies falling down.
rows.anchor: ولفظة وخروا تأبى هذين التفسيرين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says they prostrated to God in gratitude, taking the pronoun ‘to him’ as God.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: الضمير في له عائد على الله أي: خروا لله سجدا شكرا

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الداراني
rows.claim: Abu Abdullah al-Darani says prostration is only for God and argues Joseph would not have accepted it from his aged, learned, prophetic father.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الداراني: لا يكون السجود إلا لله لا ليوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says prostration was to God while Joseph served as prayer direction, like praying toward the Kaaba; Hassan’s verse illustrates the phrasing.
rows.anchor: وجعلوا يوسف قبلة كما تقول: صليت للكعبة، وصليت إلى الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret prostration as humility and kharrū as passing over rather than falling, citing the verse about not passing God’s signs deaf and blind.
rows.anchor: وقيل: السجود هنا التواضع، والخرور بمعنى المرور لا السقوط على الأرض

rows.speaker: ثابت
rows.claim: Thabit says the family’s prostration fulfilled the earlier dream; min qabl means before the intervening events.
rows.anchor: وقال ثابت: هذا تأويل رؤياي من قبل أي: سجودكم هذا تأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the parents did not literally prostrate, the dream need not be fulfilled in every detail: their journey from Canaan to Egypt for Joseph itself honored him greatly.
rows.anchor: فسجود الكواكب والشمس والقمر يعبر بتعظيم الأكابر من الناس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph was startled and his skin bristled when he saw his parents and brothers prostrate.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: أنه لما رأى سجود أبويه وإخوته هاله ذلك واقشعر جلده منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s dream came true in waking life without falsehood or idle content.
rows.anchor: أي: صادقة، رأيت ما يقع لي في المنام يقظة، لا باطل فيها ولا لغو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports conflict over the time between the dream and fulfillment, giving eighty years, eighteen years, or other figures; they also disagree about Jacob’s stay in Egypt.
rows.anchor: وفي المدة التي كانت بين رؤياه وسجودهم خلاف متناقض. قيل: ثمانون سنة، وقيل: ثمانية عشر عاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥsana normally takes ilay but can take bi as well, supported by Qurʾanic usage and poetry.
rows.anchor: وأحسن أصله أن يتعدى بإلى قال: وأحسن كما أحسن الله إليك وقد يتعدى بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ātaytanī and ʿallamtanī the final yāʾ is omitted in speech though retained in writing, its kasra standing in for it.
rows.anchor: آتيتن، وعلمتن بحذف الياء منهما اكتفاء بالكسرة عنهما، مع كونهما ثابتتين خطا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reports Ibn Dharrana’s reading rabbi ātaytanī without qad.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن عطية عن ابن ذرانة: قرأ رب آتيتني بغير قد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāṭir may describe God or be a vocative; Joseph calls God his protector in both lives, joining a transient kingdom to an enduring one.
rows.anchor: وانتصب فاطر على الصفة، أو على النداء. وأنت وليي تتولاني بالنعمة في الدارين

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Many exegetes say Joseph longed to meet God and join the righteous, seeing the world as transient; Ibn Abbas says no living person besides Joseph wished for death.
rows.anchor: وذكر كثير من المفسرين أنه لما عد نعم الله عنده تشوق إلى لقاء ربه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says no living person other than Joseph ever wished for death.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: لم يتمن الموت حي غير يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects a wish for death: Joseph asks to die Muslim when his appointed time comes and to be joined with the righteous.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنه ليس في الآية تمني الموت، وإنما عدد نعمه عليه، ثم دعا أن يتم عليه النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous may mean the people of Paradise, the prophets, or Joseph’s forefathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
rows.anchor: والصالحين أهل الجنة أو الأنبياء، أو آباؤه إبراهيم وإسحاق ويعقوب

rows.speaker: علماء التاريخ
rows.claim: Historians say Joseph lived 107 years and fathered Ephraim, Manasseh, and Rahma, Job’s wife; al-Dhahabi traces Joshua through Ephraim and Nun and recounts competing claims about Manasseh and Moses.
rows.anchor: وعلماء التاريخ يزعمون أن يوسف عليه السلام عاش مائة عام وسبعة أعوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers concede likeness only in humanity; their special qualities come from God, and they humbly describe prophethood as God’s gift to whomever He wills.
rows.anchor: سلموا لهم في أنهم يماثلونهم في البشرية وحدها، وأما ما سوى ذلك من الأوصاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s permission means His authorization and will; producing a demanded sign is outside the messengers’ power unless He wills it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى بإذن الله: بتسويغه وإرادته، أي الآية التي اقترحتموها ليس لنا الإتيان بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first command to trust initiates reliance, while the second calls them to remain steadfast; the messengers direct it first to themselves as they face hostility.
rows.anchor: والأمر الأول وهو قوله: فليتوكل المؤمنون لاستحداث التوكل، والثاني للثبات على ما استحدثوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What excuse have we not to trust God?’ points to divine guidance and enabling each person to follow the path required by religion.
rows.anchor: أي عذر لنا في أن لا نتوكل على الله وقد هدانا، فعل بنا ما يوجب توكلنا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath to be patient responds to harm already inflicted; wa mā can be a verbal noun or relative clause with its object omitted.
rows.anchor: ولنصبرن جواب قسم، ويدل على سبق ما يجب فيه الصبر وهو الأذى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads the imperative lām in li-yatawakkal with kasra, its original vowel.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: بكسر لام الأمر في ليتوكل وهو الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers threaten either expulsion or return to their religion; aw means one of the alternatives, not ‘until’ or ‘unless.’
rows.anchor: كأنهم قالوا: ليكونن أحد هذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awda may mean literal return for believers who previously followed the other religion, or becoming; the verse can address messengers and believers together.
rows.anchor: والعود هنا بمعنى الصيرورة. أو يكون خطابا للرسل ومن آمنوا بهم

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abu Haywa reads the destruction and settlement verbs in the third person, echoing ‘their Lord revealed’; direct address to believers is an honorific shift.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: ليهلكن الظالمين وليسكننكم، بياء الغيبة اعتبارا بقوله: فأوحى إليهم ربهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After disbelievers swore to expel the messengers or return them to their religion, God swears to destroy the wrongdoers and settle the messengers and believers in their land.
rows.anchor: ولما أقسموا بهم على إخراج الرسل والعودة في ملتهم، أقسم تعالى على إهلاكهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says ‘wrongdoers’ singles out those who persist, since some disbelievers might yet believe.
rows.anchor: وخص الظالمين من الذين كفروا، إذ جائز أن يؤمن من الكفرة الذين قالوا المقالة ناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes wrongdoers as polytheists; the righteous inherit their land, as promised by the verse that the outcome belongs to the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: أراد بالظالمين المشركين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ treats maqāmī as an action noun referring to God’s standing watch over people’s deeds.
rows.anchor: فقال الفراء: مقامي مصدر أضيف إلى الفاعل أي: قيامي عليه بالحفظ لأعماله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj interprets maqām as the place where people stand before God for judgment.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: مكان وقوفه بين يدي للحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent subject of ‘they sought a decision’ is the prophets, asking God for victory; it may also mean asking for judgment between the parties.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في واستفتحوا عائد على الأنبياء: أي استنصروا الله على أعدائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view includes prophets and deniers as the subject, since both sought victory for the truthful and defeat for the false.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير عائد على الفريقين: الأنبياء، ومكذبيهم، لأنهم كانوا كلهم سألوا أن ينصر المحق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read an imperative addressed to the messengers: ask your Lord for victory.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وابن محيصن: واستفتحوا بكسر التاء، أمرا للرسل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari suggests Meccans sought rain during drought after the Prophet’s prayer; instead they would receive Hell’s pus.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون أهل مكة قد استفتحوا أي استمطروا، والفتح المطر في سني القحط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Every stubborn tyrant failed’ can follow a suppressed statement that the prophets were victorious, or directly follow the disbelievers’ plea.
rows.anchor: وخاب معطوف على محذوف تقديره: فنصروا وظفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stubborn tyrants are the prophets’ opponents; ʿanīd means hostile and obstinate.
rows.anchor: وخاب كل جبار عنيد وهم قوم الرسل، وتقدم شرح جبار

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and Ibn al-Anbari interpret min warāʾihi as ‘after him’; a poem says no one can flee from God.
rows.anchor: ومن ورائه قال أبو عبيدة وابن الأنباري أي: من بعده

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وقطرب والطبري والزمخشري
rows.claim: Other authorities take min warāʾihi as ‘in front of him’; the author relates this to Hell awaiting him in worldly life or at resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة أيضا، وقطرب، والطبري، وجماعة: ومن ورائه أي ومن أمامه
